methods.description: Read the smallest instrument division or the stated rounding increment; otherwise use the smallest displayed place value. Calculate half that precision as maximum absolute error, with units. Instrument subdivisions and explicit accuracy are useful input contrasts demonstrated in example0.

Identify precision, halve it, then subtract/add the error for the two bounds. Under the explicitly stated positive-halfway-up convention include the lower endpoint and exclude the upper endpoint. Show units and both calculations.

Recover the recorded measurement as the midpoint of its bounds, the error as the distance to a bound, and precision as twice that error. This is an elementary derived inverse of the source formula, with an actual original reverse-recording task.

Compare the measurement increments to identify the more precise recorded value. Different correctly rounded readings may describe the same quantity; where compatibility is requested, compute bounds and their overlap using the taught limits method.

sourceReview.observation: The teaching explicitly identifies precision and then halves it to obtain absolute error. The source examples show $18$ kg giving precision $1$ kg and absolute error $0.5$ kg, and $18.4$ kg giving precision $0.1$ kg and absolute error $0.05$ kg. Practice includes an explicit nearest-$10$ mL instruction, supporting precedence over the displayed units place. The Key Idea concerns the subsequent percentage-error calculation, which belongs to the dependent skill. These examples and practice support one precision-and-halving method for the assigned Stage 5 skill.
sourceReview.adjustments:
Qualify the place-value rule so explicitly stated accuracy takes precedence.
Clarify that half the precision represents maximum possible rounding error.
Retain the source examples and practice values; no numerical changes are required.
